name: Gilgamesh
role: Legendary king of Uruk and the hero of the epic that bears his name
fun_fact: The epic calls him two-thirds divine and one-third human, a ratio that has puzzled and amused readers for centuries.

name: Enkidu
role: Wild man shaped by the gods to rival Gilgamesh, later his closest friend
fun_fact: The gods shaped Enkidu from clay in answer to the complaints of the people of Uruk about their king.

name: Inanna
role: Sumerian goddess of love, war, and the planet Venus, who descends to the underworld
fun_fact: Inanna is identified with the Akkadian goddess Ishtar, and the two names appear in different copies of the same stories.

name: Ereshkigal
role: Queen of the underworld, ruler of the land from which no traveller returns
fun_fact: Her Sumerian name means roughly 'Lady of the Great Earth,' and she judges the dead alongside the Anunnaki.

name: Dumuzi
role: Shepherd god and husband of Inanna, who is handed over to the underworld in her place
fun_fact: Under the Akkadian name Tammuz he was mourned in Mesopotamian rituals for well over a thousand years.

name: Marduk
role: Storm god and patron of Babylon, who defeats Tiamat and frames the world from her body
fun_fact: In Assyrian copies of Enuma Elish, the national god Ashur takes Marduk's place as the champion of the gods.

name: Tiamat
role: Primordial salt sea and mother of the gods, defeated by Marduk in the creation poem
fun_fact: In the poem her split body becomes the sky and the earth, and her eyes the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates.

name: Utnapishtim
role: Flood survivor who was granted immortality and now lives at the edge of the world
fun_fact: His name is often translated 'he found life,' and he lives with his wife at the mouth of the rivers.

name: Ea
role: God of wisdom, fresh water, and craft, who warns Utnapishtim about the flood
fun_fact: Ea is the Akkadian name of the Sumerian god Enki, whose temple stood at Eridu.

name: Humbaba
role: Monstrous guardian set by Enlil to protect the Cedar Forest
fun_fact: His face is described as coils of entrails, and his roar is compared to a flood.
